lede: Two equations in two unknowns can be written as a single matrix equation: the coefficients in a box, the unknowns in a column, the constants in another. Once it is in that shape there is nothing new to learn — it is solved with an inverse, exactly like any matrix equation.
can: Read a pair of equations straight into a coefficient matrix and two columns
Solve the matrix equation with an inverse and read the two values off
Say why the instruction to use matrices makes every other method worth nothing

text: When the question names the method

md:
You can already solve two equations in two unknowns by elimination. This topic is not about a better way; it is about what to do when the question **tells you** to use matrices.
When it does, a perfect elimination earns nothing at all. So the first thing to read is the instruction, not the equations.

prompt: One tap to begin. A question says "using a matrix method, solve these equations", and a candidate solves them correctly by elimination. What does that earn?
options: Full marks, because the answer is right
explain: A named method is part of the question. The examiners report full, correct elimination solutions scoring zero on exactly this instruction.

text: 1. Copy the numbers into three boxes

md:
The translation is mechanical. The coefficients of $x$ and $y$ go into a $2 \times 2$ box in the order they are written. The unknowns go into a column, and the constants into a column on the other side.
Nothing is worked out and nothing is cancelled. If you find yourself doing arithmetic at this stage, you are solving rather than copying.

prompt: For the pair $4x + 3y = 18$ and $2x + 5y = 16$, the coefficients go into a $2 \times 2$ matrix. What number sits in row 2, column 1 of it?
explain: Row 2 is the second equation and column 1 is the $x$ column, so it is the coefficient of $x$ there, which is $2$.

text: 2. Line them up before you copy

md:
The copying only works if both equations are in the form $ax + by = c$, with the letters in the same order on the left and the number alone on the right.
So $5x = 11 - 2y$ is rewritten as $5x + 2y = 11$ first. A missing term is a **zero**, not a gap: the box has four slots and all four are filled.

title: Why a missing term has to be a zero
md: The product multiplies row by column, so every row needs an entry in both columns to reproduce its equation. An empty slot would change the shape of the matrix, and the product would no longer be the pair you started from.

prompt: An equation in a pair reads $2y = 6$, with no term in $x$. What number goes in its $x$ slot in the coefficient matrix?
explain: Zero. Writing $0x + 2y = 6$ keeps the row complete, and the product still reproduces the equation.

text: 3. Now it is a matrix equation

md:
From here there is nothing new. The equation is $AX = B$, so $X = A^{-1}B$: find the determinant, build the inverse, and pre-multiply both sides.
The inverse goes in front of the column of constants, as always, and the product of a $2 \times 2$ with a $2 \times 1$ is the $2 \times 1$ column you are after.

prompt: The coefficient matrix for the pair above is $\begin{pmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 2 & 5\end{pmatrix}$. What is its determinant?
explain: $(4)(5) - (3)(2) = 14$. A determinant of zero would mean no unique solution.

text: 4. The column is not the answer yet

md:
The product gives a column. The question asked for two values, so name them: $x = 3$ and $y = 2$.
Then check. Put both values into **both** original equations: $4(3) + 3(2) = 18$, and the second works as well. Twenty seconds, and it catches every slip above it.

title: Summer 2025, Unit 1, Question 5
md: The inverse in part (i) was very well done. Part (ii) said to use a matrix method, and many solved by substitution or elimination instead: those answers received no marks. Of those who did use matrices, several struggled with the layout.

title: Using Matrices to Solve Simultaneous Equations - Corbettmaths
why: The whole route once, from the pair of equations to the two values, with the layout written out.

prompt: Solving a pair gives the column $\begin{pmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{pmatrix}$, where the top entry is $x$ and the bottom is $y$. What is the value of $y$?
explain: The bottom entry is $y$, so $y = 2$. Writing the column alone would leave the answer line unanswered.

text: 5. When there is no unique solution

md:
If the determinant of the coefficient matrix is zero, the matrix has no inverse and the method stops. That is not a mistake in your working: it is the pair telling you something.
Two equations whose coefficients are in the same ratio are parallel lines, so they never meet at a single point. Say that, and name the matrix whose determinant is zero.

alt: A pair of equations whose coefficient matrix has determinant zero, with the two equations shown to be multiples of one another.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 156' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The coefficient matrix of a pair whose determinant is zero, so the two equations describe parallel lines'><title>The coefficient matrix of a pair whose determinant is zero, so the two equations describe parallel lines</title><path d='M 33 42 L 24 42 L 24 110 L 33 110' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4' fill='none'/><path d='M 103 42 L 112 42 L 112 110 L 103 110' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4' fill='none'/><text x='46' y='62.4' font-family='inherit' font-size='14' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>2</text><text x='90' y='62.4' font-family='inherit' font-size='14' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>3</text><text x='46' y='96.4' font-family='inherit' font-size='14' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>4</text><text x='90' y='96.4' font-family='inherit' font-size='14' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>6</text><text x='68' y='33' font-family='inherit' font-size='11' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>coefficients</text><text x='160' y='138' font-family='inherit' font-size='11.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>every entry of row 2 is twice the entry above it, so the determinant is zero</text></svg>

prompt: The coefficient matrix of a pair of equations has determinant zero. What does that mean?
explain: No inverse exists, so the matrix method stops. The two equations describe parallel lines, which never meet at a single point.

md:
Read the instruction first, and use matrices whenever the question names them.
Line both equations up, writing a missing term as a zero.
Copy the coefficients, the unknowns and the constants into three matrices.
Solve with the inverse, in front, and read the two values off the column.
Check both values in both original equations, and say when there is no unique solution.

This comes as "find the inverse" and then "hence, using a matrix method, solve", for about $2 + 4$ marks, and the second part is locked to the matrix route. The working runs from the pair written as $AX = B$ to $x$ and $y$ named on the answer line. Stuck? Copy the coefficients into a box: once the pair is $AX = B$, the method marks are within reach.
